content.recommendations: Primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PPCI) is preferred for ST-elevation myocardial infarction; fibrinolysis if PPCI cannot be performed within 120 minutes. Patients with non-ST-elevation ACS (NSTE-ACS) with very high-risk features require immediate angiography ± PCI; other NSTE-ACS patients with high-risk features should undergo inpatient angiography (angiography within 24 h should be considered). A combination of antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is indicated acutely. Most patients with ACS will eventually undergo revascularization, most commonly with PCI. After final diagnosis, implement measures to prevent recurrent events and optimize cardiovascular risk (medical therapy, lifestyle changes, cardiac rehabilitation, psychosocial factors).
content.definitions: Acute coronary syndromes (ACS) encompass a spectrum including patients with recent changes in clinical symptoms or signs, with or without changes on 12-lead ECG and with or without acute elevations in cardiac troponin (cTn). Patients with suspected ACS may receive a diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (AMI/MI) or unstable angina (UA). The diagnosis of MI is associated with cTn release and is made using the fourth universal definition of MI. Unstable angina is myocardial ischemia at rest or with minimal exertion in the absence of acute cardiomyocyte injury/necrosis; characterized by prolonged (>20 min) rest angina, new severe angina, or angina that is increasing in frequency, duration, or lower in threshold, or occurring after a recent MI.
content.diagnostic_markers_and_tools: 12-lead ECG and cardiac troponin (cTn) concentrations are central to assessment. MI diagnosis is based on cTn release per the fourth universal definition.
content.clinical_presentations: ACS presentations range from asymptomatic at presentation to patients with ongoing chest discomfort/symptoms, cardiac arrest, electrical/haemodynamic instability, or cardiogenic shock.
